title: Making a Case
theme: Argument and persuasion: what a claim needs
objectives: I can name the parts of an argument: a claim, a thesis, reasons, and an appeal.
I can tell apart words for how strongly someone pushes for an idea, such as urge, insist, and advocate.
I can judge whether an argument is reasonable, valid, and persuasive, and explain why.
I can write a short argument with a clear thesis and one supported claim.
rationale: This first argument unit gives students the working vocabulary of persuasion (urge, advocate, insist, appeal, thesis, claim) and the tests of a sound case (reasonable, valid, persuasive). Convince is a frequent confusable with persuade, and reasonable, appeal, and claim have second senses students already know, so the unit trains them to match a word's meaning to its job in an argument. The vocabulary is reused in every essay, debate, and source evaluation later in the year.

words.def: To make someone believe something, or agree to do it, by giving good reasons.
words.ex: Eva convinced her parents to let her adopt the shelter dog by showing them a budget.
words.ex2: The lawyer tried to convince the jury that the main witness had made a mistake.
words.nonExample: Giving an order and expecting obedience does not convince anyone.

apps.academic: A strong argument convinces readers by offering evidence, not just an opinion.
apps.spoken: You've convinced me; let's try it your way.
apps.writing: Use convince when someone ends up believing or accepting something.

cloze.s: After seeing the test results, the doctor was able to ___ him that the new medicine was safe.

cloze2.s: Maya could not ___ her little brother to try the soup, even after she took a big bite herself.

misuse.s: The speaker convinced no one, so the whole audience changed their minds and cheered.
misuse.why: To convince is to win people over; if no one was convinced, no one would change their minds.

visual.alt: A speaker talking while a lightbulb glows above a listener's head.

words.def: To strongly encourage someone to do something.

senses.def: A strong wish or need to do something.
senses.example: Jo felt an urge to laugh during the silent assembly.

words.ex: The coach urged the team to stay calm during the final minute.
words.ex2: Scientists urge people to wear helmets when riding bikes.
words.nonExample: Mentioning an idea once and then walking away is not urging.

apps.academic: Writers use verbs such as urge and advocate to show how strongly a person feels.
apps.spoken: I urge you to read the instructions first.
apps.writing: Use urge when someone pushes or strongly encourages an action.

cloze.s: The mayor ___ residents to save water during the dry summer.

cloze2.s: Mom ___ me to wear a coat because the wind outside was bitter cold.

misuse.s: I urged her gently, with no feeling at all and without caring what she did.
misuse.why: To urge is to push strongly for something; not caring at all is the opposite.

visual.alt: A person with a megaphone pointing forward.

words.def: To support an idea or cause in public and work to make it happen.

senses.def: A person who publicly supports a cause.
senses.example: Dr. Lee is an advocate for clean water.

words.ex: Students advocated for a crosswalk near the school until the city built one.
words.ex2: She advocates for healthy lunches by speaking at every school board meeting.
words.nonExample: A person who watches a debate but never speaks or acts is not advocating.

apps.academic: Nonprofit groups advocate for changes in laws by writing to lawmakers.
apps.spoken: I advocate for more time to practice before the show.
apps.writing: Use advocate for support that includes speaking out or taking action.

cloze.s: The club will ___ for a new skate park by presenting a petition to the city council.

cloze2.s: Dr. Singh ___ for clean water in rural villages by raising money and speaking at conferences.

misuse.s: The senator advocated for the law by voting against it and telling reporters to ignore it.
misuse.why: To advocate for something is to support it; voting against it is the opposite.

visual.alt: A sign on a stick beside a megaphone.

words.def: Fair and sensible, and backed by sound thinking.

senses.def: Not too expensive and not too much.
senses.example: The store sells sturdy backpacks at a reasonable price.

words.ex: It is reasonable to ask for extra time when the directions were unclear.
words.ex2: The judge said the neighbor's request to keep the dog quiet at night was reasonable.
words.nonExample: Demanding a million dollars for a cup of lemonade is not reasonable.

apps.academic: A reasonable conclusion follows from the evidence you have.
apps.writing: Use reasonable for requests, decisions, and prices that are fair and sensible.

cloze.s: Asking the teacher for one more day to finish the project after a family emergency seemed ___.

cloze2.s: After the heat wave, it was ___ to hold recess indoors, since the playground was dangerously hot.

misuse.s: Demanding that everyone hand over all of their lunch money was a reasonable request.
misuse.why: A reasonable request is fair and sensible; taking everyone's lunch money is neither.

visual.alt: A balanced scale above two people shaking hands.

words.frame: A reasonable request is one that ___.

words.def: A serious request for help, support, or a change of decision.

senses.def: A quality that attracts or interests people.
senses.example: The old theater has a charm and appeal that newer buildings lack.

words.ex: The charity made an appeal for winter coats, and hundreds of people donated.
words.ex2: In a speech, an appeal to fairness reminds listeners of what is right.
words.nonExample: A casual comment that nobody answers is not an appeal.

apps.academic: Writers use appeals to emotion, logic, and trust to persuade readers.
apps.spoken: I made an appeal to my parents to extend my curfew.
apps.writing: Use appeal for a serious request, and for the charm that draws people in.

cloze.s: The coach made an ___ to parents for volunteers to drive the team to the tournament.

cloze2.s: The team's ___ for a fair rule was heard by the school board last night.

misuse.s: Her appeal was a long, funny story that did not ask anyone for anything.
misuse.why: An appeal is a serious request for help or change; a story that asks for nothing is not an appeal.

visual.alt: Hands pressed together beside a loudspeaker.

words.def: To say firmly that something is true or must be done, and refuse to back down.
words.ex: Marcus insisted that the answer was seven, even after Ms. Lee showed him the work.
words.ex2: The host insisted that we stay for dinner.
words.nonExample: Shrugging and saying 'whatever you want' is not insisting.

apps.academic: A writer who insists on a claim must provide proof.
apps.spoken: I insist on paying for lunch.
apps.writing: Use insist for firm claims or demands that the speaker will not drop.

cloze.s: Even after the referee explained the rule twice, the coach ___ that the call was wrong.

cloze2.s: Grandma ___ on carrying her own suitcase up the stairs, though we offered to help.

misuse.s: Jorge insisted he wanted to go, then added that he was happy to stay home and had no preference.
misuse.why: Insist means to firmly demand; saying you have no preference is the opposite.

visual.alt: A raised finger beside a stop sign.

words.def: Good at making people agree or act, usually by giving strong reasons.
words.ex: Her persuasive speech about recycling convinced the whole class to start a compost bin.
words.ex2: The ad was persuasive because it showed real families and clear numbers.
words.nonExample: A speech with no reasons or examples is not persuasive.

apps.academic: A persuasive essay states a claim and supports it with reasons and evidence.
apps.spoken: That's a persuasive point; I hadn't thought of it.
apps.writing: Use persuasive for writing, speech, or an argument that moves people.

cloze.s: The ___ essay gave three strong reasons and a real example for each one.

cloze2.s: Her argument was so ___ that even the doubters in the room began to nod.

misuse.s: The persuasive speech was so weak and confusing that nobody believed a word of it.
misuse.why: A persuasive speech moves people; one that nobody believes is not persuasive.

visual.alt: A person holding a microphone beside a thumbs-up.

words.def: Based on sound reasoning or facts, so it can be accepted as correct.

senses.def: Officially accepted or allowed, for example by a rule or a law.
senses.example: You need a valid ticket to enter the museum.

words.ex: Mia made a valid point when she noticed that the graph's scale started at fifty.
words.ex2: A valid argument has steps that follow one from the next.
words.nonExample: A conclusion that ignores half of the facts is not valid.

apps.academic: Scientists check whether a conclusion is valid by testing whether the data truly support it.
apps.spoken: That's a valid concern; let's check the budget.
apps.writing: Use valid for reasons or concerns that stand up when you check them.

cloze.s: Because the experiment used a fair test, the scientists felt that their conclusion was ___.

cloze2.s: Your worry about the cost is ___; let's check the budget before we decide.

misuse.s: His reason was valid, though it contained a clear error and nothing in it was true.
misuse.why: A valid reason holds up when checked; a reason with errors and no truth does not.

words.frame: A valid reason is one that ___.

words.def: The main idea or position of an essay or speech, usually stated in one sentence.
words.ex: The thesis of her essay was that every school should have a garden.
words.ex2: A strong thesis tells readers exactly what the writer will prove.
words.nonExample: A list of facts with no main point does not have a thesis.

apps.academic: Your thesis should appear in your introduction and be supported in every body paragraph.
apps.spoken: What is your thesis for the history paper?
apps.writing: Use thesis for the main claim that the whole essay supports.

cloze.s: Every paragraph in the essay supported its ___: that the town should build a safe bike path.

cloze2.s: Before writing, Ana drafted one clear sentence for her ___ and taped it above her desk.

misuse.s: His thesis was simply a list of ten random facts with no main idea.
misuse.why: A thesis states one main idea; a list of random facts does not.

visual.alt: A written page with a pin marking one sentence.

words.def: A statement that something is true, often one that still needs proof.

senses.def: A demand or request for something that belongs to you.
senses.example: She filed a claim for her lost luggage.

words.ex: The ad's claim that the sneakers make you run faster has not been proven.
words.ex2: The student supported her claim with a graph and two quotations.
words.nonExample: A question asked in class is not a claim.

apps.academic: In an argument, a claim must be backed by reasons and evidence.
apps.spoken: That's a big claim; can you prove it?
apps.writing: Use claim for a statement you plan to support, and name your evidence.

cloze.s: The ad made a bold ___ that its toothpaste would whiten teeth in one day, but it offered no proof.

cloze2.s: A good writer states a clear ___ and then backs it up with reasons and examples.

misuse.s: A claim is a question that asks for an answer and nothing else.
misuse.why: A claim is a statement that something is true, not a question.

visual.alt: A megaphone beside a question mark.

passage.title: Open the Library Earlier
paras: Dear Principal Haddad, I am writing to urge you to open our school library thirty minutes before the first bell. My thesis is simple: an earlier opening would help students learn, and it would cost the school almost nothing.

My first claim is that many students have no quiet place to work before school. Last month I surveyed one hundred twenty students in the cafeteria. Forty-one said they arrive early on the bus, and thirty-eight of those students said they would use a quiet library if it were open.

I know that some teachers insist the library staff already has too much to do. That concern is reasonable, and I do not want to add to anyone's workload. But the librarian told me that student volunteers could help check out books, and Ms. Ortiz has offered to supervise on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

Some people argue that students should simply read at home. That argument is valid for students who have a quiet room and a computer, but not everyone does. A student who shares a small apartment with three siblings may find the library is the only calm place to read. My appeal to you is based on fairness: a school should give every student a fair chance to prepare.

I understand that numbers alone may not convince everyone, so I also ask you to picture a student finishing an assignment in a quiet corner at 7:45. That picture is persuasive only because it is true for students in our school. Please consider a one-month trial. I will gladly advocate for it at the next student council meeting. Thank you for considering my request.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "thesis" most nearly means
choices: the main idea the writer will support
a question the writer wants answered
a list of the writer's favorite books
a thank-you to the principal
qs.why: Amara states her main position right after the word thesis: an earlier opening would help students learn.

qs.q: Which detail best supports Amara's claim that students would use an earlier library?
choices: Ms. Ortiz can supervise on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
She surveyed one hundred twenty students in the cafeteria.
Thirty-eight of the forty-one students who arrive early said they would use it.
The librarian said volunteers could help check out books.
qs.why: Only the survey result about early arrivals shows that students would actually use the library; the other details answer different questions.

qs.q: Why does Amara mention that volunteers and Ms. Ortiz could help?
choices: She wants to show that the librarian does not work hard.
She wants to answer the worry that the staff already has too much to do.
She wants to prove that students prefer volunteering.
She is asking for Ms. Ortiz to be promoted.
qs.why: Amara first admits the concern about staff workload is reasonable, then offers a solution to it.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the phrase "That argument is valid" most nearly means that the argument
choices: is sound for some students
is too long to read
is written in a polite style
has been officially approved by the school
qs.why: Amara accepts that reading at home makes sense for students who have a quiet room, but points out that not everyone does.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the letter?
choices: Students should read at home instead of at school.
Principals should listen to every request without question.
Opening the library earlier would be fair and helpful, and a trial could prove it.
The school library needs a new librarian.
qs.why: The letter states a thesis, gives claims, answers objections, and asks for a one-month trial.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for building and judging an argument, read a student letter to a principal, practice telling apart words for how strongly someone pushes for an idea, and write a short argument with a thesis, a claim, and a reason.

notes.va.convince.v: Convince is traditionally about belief (I convinced him it was true) and persuade about action (I persuaded him to go), though the two are often used the same way. Use the contrast as a mini-lesson but do not turn it into a rule students will be graded on.
notes.va.urge.v: Urge sits between suggest and demand. It also names an inner feeling (an urge to laugh). Students may confuse urge with urgent; they are related by the idea of pushing.
notes.va.advocate.v: As a verb the last syllable rhymes with 'ate'; as a noun it is reduced. Advocate implies action over time, more than simply agreeing. Ask: what is the difference between supporting a cause and advocating for it?
notes.va.reasonable.adj: Reasonable relates to reason: a reasonable idea has reasons behind it. Note the second sense, a fair price, which students meet in shopping contexts. Reasonable does not mean 'agrees with me'.
notes.va.appeal.n: Teach the noun sense (a request or plea) first and then the sense of attraction (the appeal of a game). Connect to persuasion: an appeal to fairness or to emotion is a request that targets a value.
notes.va.insist.v: Insist is firmer than urge: the speaker will not back down. Students may think insist is rude; it can be polite (a host who insists). Insisting does not prove a claim: ask whether insisting makes an argument stronger.
notes.va.persuasive.adj: Persuasive describes whether an argument works on an audience; valid describes whether the reasoning holds. A persuasive argument can be invalid (a good speaker with bad reasoning), which is worth discussing.
notes.va.valid.adj: Valid asks whether reasons hold up. In math and logic it has a stricter meaning; keep it to everyday argument here. The second sense, an accepted ticket or ID, is a helpful bridge.
notes.va.thesis.n: A thesis is a claim for a whole piece of writing; a claim can be a smaller step inside the argument. The plural is theses (pronounced THEE-seez).
notes.va.claim.n: Claim is the building block of argument: a statement that could be true or false and needs evidence. Students often state facts instead of claims; ask whether someone could disagree. The second sense (an insurance claim) appears in real-world texts.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Amara writes, My thesis is simple, so I know that is her main idea for the whole letter. Then she says, My first claim is, which is one step that supports it. The numbers from her survey are the evidence. A thesis is the whole idea, a claim is one part of the case.'
discuss: Which part of a persuasive argument matters most: the claim, the evidence, or the appeal? Why?
How can you tell the difference between a reasonable request and an unreasonable one?
misconceptions: A claim is a fact that everyone already agrees on.
Insist and urge mean the same thing.
A persuasive argument is automatically a valid one.
extend: Read two short ads and decide which is more persuasive, then explain whether each is valid.
Write a thesis sentence for three different topics, then trade with a partner and ask whether each could be disputed.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Link back to skeptical, candid, inconsistent, and evident from units 1 to 3: ask students how a skeptical reader would test a claim and what makes a reason evident or inconsistent. Quick recall at two days and one week.

frames: That reason is valid because ___, but this one is not valid because ___.
wida.oral: Partner A states a claim about school or home. Partner B asks for a reason, then says whether it is valid and persuasive.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: instar (urge; 'exhortar' also possible), abogar (usually 'abogar por'), petición (appeal; 'llamamiento' also possible), afirmación (claim), razonable.
Sense boundary: convince vs persuade is described as a traditional distinction that is often blurred; confirm the teacher note is accurate and not too prescriptive.
Second senses taught for urge (noun), advocate (noun), reasonable (fair price), appeal (attraction), valid (officially accepted), claim (insurance or ownership claim): confirm each is helpful.
Passage is a fictional letter; the survey numbers (120 students, 41 early arrivals, 38 who would use the library) are invented and internally consistent.
